extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy; readers interested in foundations of ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and evaluation of candidate bases for moral theory (consciousness/conscience, metaphysical grounding, psychological facts), and criteria for moral worth of actions as argued by Schopenhauer. The page presents definitions, tests, and empirical/historical confirmations used to judge moral foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective basis of morals (academy demand)
rubrics_metrics.description: The basis of morality sought must be the objectively true, ultimate foundation of morals — an account independent of every positive law, improved assumption, or external prop; the Academy asks for a theoretical, not practical, exposition of the ultimate basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator/author emphasises the Royal Society's requirement for a purely philosophical, objective, and undisguised exposition of morality's ultimate foundation; such a basis should not be merely a practical manual or rooted in contingent rewards/punishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of Ethics: explain, not prescribe
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethics' aim is not to teach what people 'ought' to do (the 'ought' belonging to theological morals), but to 'point out all the varied moral lines of human conduct; to explain them; and to trace them to their ultimate source.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer treats Ethics as descriptive/diagnostic: the metric for success is explanatory power in tracing moral phenomena to their source, rather than giving prescriptive commands. Anti-pattern: treating ethics primarily as a set of imperatives without account of origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphysical grounding required for exhaustive account
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete and exhaustive foundation of morals ultimately presupposes metaphysics; metaphysics must precede moral philosophy because the final ethical significance of action connects to the ultimate nature of the universe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites Wolff and Kant: without metaphysical illumination, practical philosophy remains in darkness. If one demands an account that is more than psychological description, it must attach to a system of metaphysics (synthetic method).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological constraint: analytic vs synthetic approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: If ethics is to be treated independently of metaphysics (as the Society requires), the analytic method (starting from facts of experience or consciousness) must be used; if attached to metaphysics, the synthetic method (deducing ethics from metaphysical first principles) is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a methodological rubric: recognizing which method is appropriate shapes what counts as acceptable evidence or proof. Analytic accounts must accept the limitation that the ultimate origin may remain psychological or primitive datum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of moral worth: absence of egoistic motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate test of truly moral conduct is the absence of all egoistic motivation; genuinely moral acts occur without the slightest hope of reward or fear of punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer treats the absence of egoistic incentive as the criterion for moral worth. Examples/anti-patterns: acts done solely for praise, reward, or to avoid punishment are not truly moral; partial mixtures of egoism and compassion reduce moral worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Duties are defined as 'actions, the simple omission of which constitutes a wrong.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a working definition used to identify duties: if failing to perform an action would itself be wrong, that action counts as a duty. Use this to classify obligations and distinguish duties from optional praiseworthy acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antimoral incentives: Egoism and Malice
rubrics_metrics.description: Two fundamental 'antimoral' incentives in human nature are identified: Egoism and Malice (the latter may be regarded as extreme egoism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer treats these as the principal counter-motives to morality; any account of moral action must explain how these incentives are countered or transformed. Anti-pattern: ignoring malice as a distinct phenomenon or reducing all behavior to benign motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compassion as the sole non-egoistic moral incentive
rubrics_metrics.description: Compassion (the sense of 'suffering with' another) is asserted as the only true non-egoistic source of moral action and thus the sole fountain of genuine morality; justice and loving-kindness are manifestations of compassion at lower and higher degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Schopenhauer's central normative criterion: when evaluating moral theories or explaining moral actions, check whether they identify compassion (not duty, utility, or obedience) as the non-egoistic spring. He offers logical argumentation and empirical confirmations in support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical confirmation (imaginary case) supporting compassion
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of hypothetical/imaginary cases to illustrate why compassion must be the moral incentive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of nine empirical/supportive considerations Schopenhauer adduces. Such thought-experiments serve as tests of intuitions about motive and moral worth; include them when arguing for compassion's primacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cruelty marks deepest moral depravity (absence of compassion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cruelty, understood as maximum deficiency in compassion, is the mark of the deepest moral depravity; this empirical observation supports compassion as the root of morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat cruelty as an empirical indicator: if lack of compassion correlates with moral depravity across cases, that supports compassion-as-root. Use cross-cultural and historical examples as corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compassion is the only thoroughly effective spring of moral conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Compassion is empirically the only motive that reliably produces moral conduct, i.e., it is uniquely effective in motivating justice and loving-kindness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating rival motives (duty, self-interest, fear of punishment), test their empirical effectiveness relative to compassion—Schopenhauer argues compassion outperforms them in producing genuine moral action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitless compassion as a token of a really good person
rubrics_metrics.description: An unbounded or extensive compassion for all living things is taken as the surest and most certain token of genuine moral goodness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functions as a diagnostic criterion: the broader and less partial a person's compassion, the stronger evidence they are morally good. Anti-pattern: restricting compassion to in-group only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine-grained empirical details corroborate compassion
rubrics_metrics.description: Various separate matters of detail in experience and literature provide supporting evidence for compassion being the moral source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer lists multiple small empirical confirmations (examples from texts, practices) that cumulatively strengthen the claim; evaluators should consider breadth of supporting data, not rely on single anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compassion more discernible in higher manifestations (loving-kindness) than in justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Compassion is more obviously the root of loving-kindness (higher power) than of justice (lower power); the motive shows more clearly in some virtues than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use differential clarity among virtues as a test: where motive is most transparent (loving-kindness), compassion's role is easier to detect; where motives are institutionalized (justice), the connection may be more indirect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compassion extends beyond humans to all living beings
rubrics_metrics.description: Compassion does not stop with human beings but includes all living things; this universality supports its claim as the fundamental moral incentive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an account of morality can account for moral intimations toward animals and plants; universality of motive strengthens its plausibility as fundamental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compassion as empirical antidote to egoism and remedy for suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: From the empirical point of view, compassion is the best antidote to egoism and the most soothing balm for the world's inevitable suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical evaluators should consider whether fostering compassion reduces egoistic behavior and alleviates suffering more effectively than alternatives (law, deterrence, utility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and cross-cultural testimony as supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimonies from Rousseau, Pañcatantra, Pausanias, Lucian, Stobaeus, Lessing, Chinese Ethics, Hindu customs, etc., are cited as historical/cross-cultural evidence for compassion's centrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistency of moral sentiment across texts, traditions, and cultures as a corroborative metric; broad attestation across sources increases plausibility of compassion as foundational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical difference of character explained by intelligible vs empirical character
rubrics_metrics.description: The ethical difference between individuals is treated as innate/ultimate and explained via Kant's distinction: the Intelligible Character (noumenal) is transcendentally free while the Empirical Character (phenomenal) is determined—this accounts for enduring differences in moral character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a metaphysical criterion for explaining variance in moral dispositions: an acceptable moral foundation should either explain (or at least accommodate) persistent individual differences in moral character; Schopenhauer appeals to Kantian metaphysics to do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of theological/reward-punishment foundations for moral worth
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions performed solely from threat of punishment or promise of reward are not truly moral but egoistic in root; therefore a theological grounding that reduces morality to such incentives fails the test of moral worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing moral systems, test whether they reduce morality to incentives (rewards/punishments) — if so, they fail Schopenhauer's criterion for genuine morality. This is used to critique theological and some Kantian readings.
